summary.text: The Cretaceous Kuparuk River field on the North Slope of Alaska is the second largest oil field in North America.
Sequence stratigraphy correlations revealed that the A unit consists of six separate sandstone bodies prograding northeastward, separated by marine shales.

how_it_works.text: The Cretaceous Kuparuk River field on the North Slope of Alaska is the second largest oil field in North America, with 6BBSTOOIP.
As of 2006, 2BBO had been produced from two intervals, named the A and C units.
In the early days of field development each unit was considered a laterally continuous sandstone body.
Sequence stratigraphy correlations revealed that the A unit consists of six separate sandstone bodies that prograded in the seaward (northeast) direction.
Each of the six sandstone bodies in the A unit is separated by a high-frequency transgressive marine shale.

steps.text: Initially, the field development treated each unit as a single laterally continuous sandstone body.
Later, sequence stratigraphy correlations demonstrated that the A unit comprises six separate sandstone bodies prograding in the northeast direction.

numbers.text: Initial volume parameters and production numbers include 6BBSTOOIP total and 2BBO produced as of 2006 from the A and C units.

right.text: Detailed sequence stratigraphy can reveal that a seemingly uniform unit actually consists of multiple separate sandstone bodies separated by shales.

data_meaning.input: Well logs and sequence stratigraphy correlation data.
data_meaning.output: Identification of separate sandstone bodies (units A1-A6) and intervening marine shales.

breaks.text: Assuming a single laterally continuous reservoir body without performing sequence stratigraphy correlation leads to compartmentalization errors.

hypotheses.text: Гипотеза: Разделение единого пласта на изолированные тела улучшает точность предиктивных моделей разработки.
